messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Ship Captain
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 52

Margaret sits in the chair across from me with the straight-backed posture of someone used to commanding a bridge. Her hands, gnarled by decades of salt and rope, rest motionless on her thighs. She is seventy-six years old, a widow for eight years, and until last spring, she was still piloting her own coastal freighter out of Rotterdam—a small vessel she had captained for over forty years. But she sold the ship after the incident, and now she spends most days in her flat overlooking the harbour, watching other boats come and go.

The trauma happened on a Tuesday evening in April, a little over a year ago. She had docked in a port city she knew well, a place where she often picked up cargo. She needed a few supplies before the next leg—nothing urgent. She walked to a corner market a few blocks from the quay. On her way back, she saw two police officers struggling with a young man on the pavement. He was facedown, wrists being twisted behind his back. Margaret stopped, instinctively, because she has always believed in watching the sea and the land with equal attention. She did not shout. She did not intervene. She simply stood there, holding her bag of provisions, and watched.

One of the officers looked up and saw her watching. He said something to his partner. Then he walked toward her, his hand resting on his belt. He was close enough that she could smell coffee on his breath. “Move along, grandma,” he said, and when she did not move immediately—just a hesitation, a beat of surprise—he shoved her. Not a push to make her fall, but a shove to the shoulder that sent her stumbling sideways into a wall. Her bag dropped. A tin of tomatoes rolled into the gutter. She looked up at him, and he was already turning away, back to the arrest. She picked up her things and walked back to the ship. Her hands were shaking, but she told herself it was nothing—a rudeness, a misunderstanding. She did not report it. She did not tell anyone. That night, she woke up at 3 a.m. with her heart hammering, sure she heard boots on the gangway.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret found herself avoiding the portside streets where she had always walked freely. She began checking the locks on her cabin door three times before sleeping. Small sounds—a raised voice on the dock, a car door slamming—made her freeze mid-step. She started drinking more coffee to stay alert, then more wine to fall asleep. Her crew noticed she was sharp with them, snapping over minor things. She stopped going ashore during layovers. When a customs officer boarded for a routine inspection, her throat closed and she had to excuse herself to the head. She felt ashamed. She had navigated storms, engine fires, and a mutiny attempt in her younger years. Why should a shove from a man with a badge undo her?

The last straw came when she nearly collided with a buoy in calm water because she was staring at a police launch on the horizon, wondering if it would come alongside. She realized she was no longer safe to command. She sold the ship to a younger captain, packed her sea bag, and moved into the flat.

Now, she sits with me and tells me these things in a flat, even voice. She does not cry. She says she has no nightmares, but then adds that she wakes up every night at the same hour, drenched, with the image of a black boot coming toward her face. She says she does not think about the incident during the day, but she has stopped wearing the navy peacoat she used to love because it reminds her of the uniform of the officer. She says she is fine. She says she just needed someone to talk to, because her daughters think she is becoming paranoid. She looks out my window, which faces a quiet street, and she flinches when a car backfires in the distance.
